content: Have you ever noticed how your tiffin gets empty in 5 minutes when you share it with friends, but takes 30 minutes to finish at home alone? Why does food taste so much better when we eat together?

Socratic Question: Imagine a school where students study together but are not allowed to eat together. How would they feel? Why do you think the government started cooking food in schools for children?

content.title: The Mid-Day Meal Journey
content.description: An animation showing fresh vegetables arriving at a school, being cooked in large vessels, and served to students sitting in rows.

content: The Supreme Court of India ordered that all children in primary school must be provided with hot, cooked food. This is called the **Mid-Day Meal** scheme. In some schools, like **Boarding Schools**, children even live, study, and eat all their meals together in a large dining hall!

description: A free, cooked meal provided to children in government schools to ensure they get proper nutrition.

question: Which of the following is true about the Mid-Day Meal scheme?
options: Every primary school child has a right to a hot, cooked meal
Students have to pay for it
It is only served once a year

content: Reflection: Ask students what their favorite mid-day meal or tiffin item is. Discussing shared meals builds a sense of equality, as everyone eats the exact same food regardless of their background.

Connection: Just like how students eat together at school, entire families and communities eat together during special occasions and festivals. This brings us to how big community feasts are prepared.
Mastery Task: Design a healthy menu for your school's Mid-Day Meal for one whole week. Make sure to include vegetables, dal, and rice or roti!

Imagine a kitchen where the pots are so big that you could fit a bicycle inside them! Hundreds of people are chopping vegetables, making rotis, and serving food, but nobody is getting paid. How is this possible?
Socratic Question: If thousands of people come to eat at a temple, who pays for the food, and who does all the cooking?

content.title: The Mega Kitchen
content.description: An animation showing the massive scale of a Gurudwara kitchen: giant tandoors baking hundreds of rotis at once and huge vats of dal simmering.

content: In a Gurudwara, a free meal is served to everyone, rich or poor, sitting together on the floor. This is called a **Langar**. The food is cooked and served by volunteers. This voluntary service is called **Seva**. During festivals like **Bihu** in Assam, villages also organize community feasts called *Bhoj*.

description: A communal free kitchen in a Gurudwara where everyone sits together on the floor and eats.
Selfless service performed without any expectation of a reward.

content: Students often think Langar is only for poor people. Truth: Langar is for EVERYONE. Rich, poor, kings, and commoners all sit together at the same level to eat, showing that everyone is equal.

question: The voluntary work of cooking and serving food in a Gurudwara is known as:

content: Reflection: Why do you think everyone sits on the floor to eat in a Langar? It teaches us humility and equality—nobody is higher or lower.

Connection: This idea of equality and community service is a core part of ancient Indian culture, dating back to Vedic traditions of 'Annadaan' (the gift of food). You will see this again when learning about Indian history and festivals.

Mastery Challenge: Create a step-by-step plan to organize a mini-Langar (community feast) in your neighborhood. Write down what food you will serve, who will do the 'Seva' of cooking, and who will clean up!
